title: The Impact of Workplace Gaslighting from Colleagues on Greek Nurses’ Mental Health and Professional Life
content: OBJECTIVE To examine the association between workplace gaslighting from colleagues and nurses' mental health and professional life. METHOD We conducted an online cross-sectional study with a convenience sample of 92 nurses in Greece between August and September 2026. We measured gaslighting from colleagues with the colleagues version of the Gaslighting at Work Scale. We measured anxiety and depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-4, work engagement with the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale-3, job burnout with the single item burnout measure, and job satisfaction, turnover intention, perceived quality of care and patient safety with single items. We performed multivariable linear, binary logistic and ordinal logistic regression analyses, adjusting for gender, age, understaffing, shift work and postgraduate education. RESULTS Overall, 76.1% of nurses experienced high levels of gaslighting from colleagues. After adjustment for confounders, higher gaslighting scores were associated with lower job satisfaction (b=−0.52, 95% confidence interval [CI]=−0.87 to −0.18) and work engagement (b=−0.48, 95% CI=−0.75 to −0.22), and with higher job burnout (b=0.73, 95% CI=0.30 to 1.16), turnover intention (b=0.73, 95% CI=0.40 to 1.06), anxiety (b=0.83, 95% CI=0.50 to 1.16) and depression (b=0.79, 95% CI=0.41 to 1.17). Each one-unit increase in the gaslighting score increased the odds of a positive screen for anxiety (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]=4.97, 95% CI=2.29 to 10.80) and depression (aOR=3.13, 95% CI=1.65 to 5.95), and of high turnover intention (aOR=3.57, 95% CI=1.67 to 7.61). CONCLUSIONS Gaslighting from colleagues was common among Greek nurses and was associated with poorer mental health and adverse professional outcomes. Healthcare organizations should recognize peer gaslighting as a distinct occupational hazard and implement policies to prevent it.
